To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the protective effect of barbituratic anesthesia during incomplete ischemia is not due to an increase in cerebral blood flow during the initial recircluation phase nor to a decrease in oxygen utilization rate during the postischemic recovery period.
the protective effects previously reported of the barbiturates against ischemia-induced cerebral energy failure is due to a reduction in cerebral energy utilization.
the protective effect of phenobarbittal in this model of cerebral ischemia is not due to a decrease in cerebral oxygen consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of anesthesia on postischemic recovery of the brain in the rat.
the development of a method for the determination of cerebral blood flow in rats.
the study of cerebral energy metabolism during and after transient ischemia in rats, with particular emphasis on the effects of different types of anesthesia on cerebral metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results do not indicate that the failure of recovery in the N2O group was due to impaired recirulation or due to a reduced CMRo2.
, at least in this particular experimental situation, the protective effect of phenobarbittal is not due to an increased postischemic blood flow, nor is it primarily due to a reduction of CMRo2.

, in the rat, 30 min of transient, incomplete ischemia does not cause a grossly inhomogeneous pattern of blood flow and metabolism, and that the protective effects previously reported for barbiturates are not due to an increased postischemic blood flow and oxygen extraction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the present model of incomplete cerebral ischemia does not seem to be suitable to test the protective effects of anesthetics.

phenobarbital protects the brain against the consequences of ischemia by a direct effect on the cerebral metabolic state, whereas N2O does not have this effect and is therefore a poor anesthetic for the protection of the brain against the effects of ischemia.

the protective effects obtained with barbiturates in this model of incomplete cerebral ischemia are not due to their ability either to reduce cerebral energy consumption or to increase cerebral perfusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the model of incomplete ischemia studied, phenobarbital does not exert its protective action by increasing rCBF.

the effects of anesthetic agents on the outcome of cerebral ischemia are multifactorial and that the use of a specific anesthetic agent in an experimental model of cerebral ischemia should not be based on the results obtained in a single study.
the use of 70% N 2O as anesthetic agent in experimental models of cerebral ischemia may be a poor choice.
